issues.description: The Experiment 1 procedure states participants used a 2-point confidence scale ('from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain'), yet the Analysis section describes the same scale as running from 1 to 4 ('1 = guess, 4 = certainty'). These are incompatible descriptions of the same measure. This ambiguity makes it impossible to know what threshold was used to define 'high confidence' and undermines the entire analytical strategy, which depends on isolating high-confidence responses.
issues.quote: participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain) … Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 1 – 3: anecdotal evidence … [Analysis header:] 1 = guess, 4 = certainty

issues.subcategory: direct contradiction between text and table
issues.description: In the Experiment 2 results, the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay),' implying very strong evidence for a memory-delay effect on non-illusory errors. However, Table 4, which is explicitly presented for this analysis, shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay—strong evidence AGAINST including memory delay. These two numbers directly contradict each other, indicating either a copy-paste error from a different analysis or a fundamental mis-reporting of the statistical results.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42 … Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) … Table 4: Memory Delay | BFincl = 0.064

issues.description: In Experiment 1, 45 participants started training and 5 were excluded, leaving 40. After the main experiment, the analysis section reports that 23 participants were included and 5 were excluded based on too-few high-confidence trials, giving 28. However, 40 − 28 = 12 participants are entirely unaccounted for. No explanation is provided for these 12 missing participants, violating CONSORT-style transparency and raising concerns about undisclosed additional exclusion criteria.
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants … Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Letters are uniquely verbal stimuli that participants routinely rehearse by their phonological name (e.g., silently saying 'C'). No articulatory suppression task was employed, so what is claimed to be purely visual short-term memory is inextricably mixed with verbal working memory. Verbal rehearsal of the letter name would naturally produce a real-letter representation, trivially explaining pseudo-to-real illusions without invoking predictive processing or world knowledge about visual form. The manuscript does not control for or even adequately discuss this major confound.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet … Here, we present 4 experiments that test whether STM is susceptible to illusory memories … high confidence reports of having seen a real letter when a pseudo-letter was shown

issues.subcategory: interference display presented after the retro-cue
issues.description: In the Short and Long conditions of Experiment 1, the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory-display offset, yet the retro-cue appeared at 0.75 s (Short) or 3 s (Long). Because the cue preceded the interference display, participants already knew which item to retain when the interfering stimulus appeared. This means the second display did not interfere with pre-cue memory storage in those conditions, fundamentally undermining the manipulation of 'interference before cue.' Interference only co-occurred with the cue in the Short-with-Interference condition, making cross-condition comparisons about decay vs. interference uninterpretable.
issues.quote: If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset, which meant that the interval between the probe and the irrelevant second display was either presented for 1.5s (Long delay) or 3.75s (short delay). In all cases, the memory probe was shown for 0.5 seconds … after offset of the second letter display, the participant first indicated the identity of the letter

issues.description: All responses in Experiment 1 occur after the second display (at ~5.5 s post-memory-display). The only manipulation is when the retro-cue appeared (0.75 s vs. 3 s). If what matters for illusions is the delay before response, this is identical across conditions; if what matters is delay before cueing, that differs but has alternative interpretations (retro-cueing benefit, not memory decay). The manuscript treats this as a straightforward memory-delay manipulation, but the design actually conflates retro-cueing timing with memory delay.
issues.quote: In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display … after offset of the second letter display, the participant first indicated the identity of the letter at the cued location in the memory display

issues.description: In Experiment 1, when the target was a pseudo-letter, the actual pseudo-letter appeared as a response option on only 50% of such trials; on the other 50%, only the real counterpart was available. This means on half of pseudo-letter-target trials, a correct response was impossible, which mechanically inflates pseudo-to-real 'illusion' rates. The asymmetry is not mirrored for real-letter targets (the real letter was available on 83% of such trials). This design artifact produces an upward bias in the key comparison supporting the world-knowledge hypothesis.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials

issues.subcategory: high exclusion rate introducing selection bias
issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded because they had fewer than 10 high-confidence trials in at least one cell. Included participants had nearly triple the confidence rate of excluded participants (49.2% vs. 15.7%). This is not random attrition: it systematically removes participants with lower metacognitive confidence or more cautious response strategies. The remaining sample is not representative of the enrolled population, inflating apparent effect sizes and limiting generalizability.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) … Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions … Excluded participants had on average 15.7% high confidence trials

issues.subcategory: high confidence is not validated as a marker of illusory memory
issues.description: The central analytical strategy rests on treating high-confidence errors as evidence of genuine 'illusory memories' rather than guesses. However, high confidence in wrong answers can arise from at least three alternative mechanisms not distinguished here: (1) systematic perceptual biases that operate deterministically regardless of memory; (2) criterion-shifting, where participants lower their confidence threshold when reporting the expected (real-letter) option; (3) metacognitive miscalibration. Without validation that high-confidence errors actually reflect a subjectively vivid false memory (e.g., using a 'Remember/Know' paradigm or asking participants to report phenomenal qualities of the memory), the core construct is unvalidated.
issues.quote: Focusing on memory illusions instead of general false memory reports allows a separation of such incorrect but seemingly true memories from memory lapses that are filled in by best guesses … isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom breakout rooms and the Neurotask platform, while Experiments 1–3 were run in controlled laboratory settings. Browser-based timing is known to be imprecise (variable by tens of milliseconds), viewing distance was uncontrolled, and ambient lighting, screen type, and screen resolution varied across participants. For a study critically dependent on precise stimulus presentation timing (250 ms memory display, 500 ms delays) and accurate measurement of STM, these uncontrolled variables are serious threats to internal validity and to cross-experiment comparisons.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: confound between delay and interference in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 has three conditions: Short (delay 0.75 s, no interference), Short-with-Interference (delay 0.75 s, interfering display), and Long (delay 3 s, no interference). Because no condition combines a long delay WITH interference, and no condition isolates interference from delay, the separate contributions of temporal decay and visual interference on illusion rate cannot be independently estimated. The authors treat these as additive factors, but the design precludes testing that assumption.
issues.quote: If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition). If the probe was presented 3 seconds after offset of the memory display (the Long condition), it appeared in isolation.

issues.description: The training task used simple rectangles varying in orientation (horizontal, vertical, oblique), requiring change detection. The experimental task required identifying specific letter identities (real vs. mirror-reversed). These tasks involve very different cognitive processes: basic orientation discrimination vs. categorical letter recognition. The 75% accuracy criterion on the training task does not validate competence on the experimental task, and the training could implicitly prime orientation-change detection rather than letter-identity judgment.
issues.quote: Prior to the main experiment, participants were trained on a cued change detection task … The memory and test displays each consisted of eight white rectangles … orientations were pseudo-randomly selected … Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct … on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.subcategory: directional distinction collapsed in the error-type factor
issues.description: The analysis collapses pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo illusions into a single 'illusory error' category for the main ANOVA. While the target-type × error-type interaction partially recovers directionality, combining these two qualitatively different error directions obscures potentially asymmetric dynamics across conditions. For example, if pseudo-to-real illusions increase strongly with delay while real-to-pseudo illusions do not, this asymmetry is invisible in the main analysis and must be inferred from post-hoc comparisons.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: null result of cue-color manipulation inadequately explained
issues.description: A primary novel hypothesis in Experiment 2 — that transiently induced expectations (via cue color) would modulate illusion rates — was not supported (BFincl = 0.07 for cue color). The post-hoc explanation offered ('expectations need substantial time to develop') is untested and unfalsified within the paper. The failure of the manipulation is acknowledged but then set aside without investigating whether participants were even aware of the cue-probability contingency (the questionnaire revealed they were not, but this is reported only in passing and not treated as a manipulation check failure).
issues.quote: However, transiently generated expectations, in this case provided by a cue about the prevalence of real versus pseudo-letters targets, had no effect on the prevalence of illusory memories. This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.description: The manuscript references 'Figure 5' for both Experiment 3 results ('Figure 5 Experiment 3. Error rates…') and Experiment 4 results ('Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials'). A figure cannot serve double-duty for two separate experiments. Either one figure was mislabeled or a figure was omitted. This error disrupts the traceability of results to figures.
issues.quote: Figure 5 Experiment 3. Error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence in their response … [Experiment 4 Results:] Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: Experiment 3 used a stopping rule of BF > 6 while Experiment 4 used BF > 10, both for the same critical t-test. No justification is provided for why these thresholds differ across otherwise parallel experiments. Changing the stopping rule between experiments could reflect post-hoc criterion adjustment. Additionally, neither stopping rule was pre-registered, raising concerns about researcher degrees of freedom even within the Bayesian sequential framework.
issues.quote: once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop [Experiment 3] … once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop [Experiment 4]

issues.subcategory: perception vs. memory distinction is conceptually inconsistent with the invoked theory
issues.description: The authors use the increase in illusions over time to argue that illusions are 'memory-based' not 'perception-based.' However, they simultaneously advocate a predictive-processing framework in which perception and memory operate via the same Bayesian inference mechanism. Within predictive processing, the distinction between a 'perceptual error' and a 'memory error' is not well-defined: memory maintenance can be viewed as continued perceptual inference over time. The argument thus presupposes a perception/memory dichotomy that is undercut by the very theoretical framework invoked to explain the results.
issues.quote: the increase in memory illusions over time suggests that, in our experiments, participants mainly start out with a correct percept … How can world knowledge shape the memory of events that have only just been removed from vision? One possibility is that both perception and cognitive processes such as STM operate according to Bayesian principles … 'predictive processing'

issues.subcategory: world knowledge explanation is unoperationalized and unmeasured
issues.description: The authors attribute the pseudo-to-real asymmetry to 'world knowledge' — participants' prior experience with correctly oriented letters — but never independently measure or quantify prior strength. The claim that priors for real letters are stronger than priors for pseudo-letters is assumed, not demonstrated. Without individual-difference measures of prior strength (e.g., reading experience, letter-familiarity ratings, or computational estimates of prior probability), the world-knowledge account cannot be distinguished from other explanations such as differential encoding difficulty or categorical familiarity.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet. Previous experience with letters should have provided participants with abundant evidence that letters typically appear in their standard form. This should provide strong internal expectations about the appearance of the letters of the alphabet.

issues.subcategory: no baseline or perceptual control measure
issues.description: The experiments have no condition with zero delay (simultaneous probe) or a probe during stimulus presentation, which would establish a genuine perceptual baseline. Without this, the error rates at the earliest delay (0.75 s) are already potentially contaminated by early memory processes, and there is no anchor point that unambiguously reflects pure perceptual encoding. The authors acknowledge that 'perceptual illusions can, at best, account for a small number of incorrect responses,' but this is a quantitative claim made without any direct measurement.
issues.quote: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM – since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed.

issues.description: Throughout all four experiments, the text repeatedly references 'Appendix 1 for full model comparison,' but no Appendix 1 is provided in the manuscript. Without access to the complete model comparison tables, readers cannot independently evaluate which models were considered, verify that the best-fitting model was correctly identified, or assess whether model selection was conducted transparently.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison and Table 1 for an overview of BFincl … see Appendix 1 for full model comparison and Table 2 … see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4

issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned for Experiments 1 or 2. Given the multiple analytic decisions involved (participant exclusion criteria, confidence thresholds, collapsing over conditions, choice of follow-up tests), the absence of pre-registration substantially increases the risk of researcher degrees of freedom inflating reported Bayes Factors. This is particularly relevant because the experiments were exploratory in nature and produced one null result (cue-color manipulation).
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis … [Only for Experiments 3 and 4; no equivalent statement for Experiments 1 and 2]

issues.description: The training stimuli are described as 'eight white rectangles (0.05° × 0.01° in size).' At a standard viewing distance of ~60 cm, 0.05° subtends approximately 0.05 mm — far below acuity thresholds and essentially invisible. The unit is almost certainly wrong (likely cm or mm, not degrees of visual angle) and was never corrected in the main experiment description. This prevents replication of the stimulus parameters.
issues.quote: The memory and test displays each consisted of eight white rectangles (0.05◦ × 0.01◦ in size) which had horizontal, vertical or oblique (45° or 135°) orientations.

issues.subcategory: stimulus set restricted to asymmetric letters without discussion of generalizability
issues.description: Symmetric letters (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y) were excluded because mirroring them produces identical stimuli. This removes 11 of the 26 English letters (~42%), leaving a non-representative subset. The remaining letters may differ systematically from excluded letters in frequency, visual complexity, or prior familiarity. The implications of this stimulus restriction for the generalizability of the findings are not discussed.
issues.quote: only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays)

issues.description: The cutoff of 10 high-confidence trials per cell is presented without any power-analysis justification. Given that the total number of critical trials per cell varies across experiments and conditions, the same absolute threshold has different relative implications. No sensitivity analysis is reported to test whether results change if the threshold is varied (e.g., 5 or 15 trials), making it impossible to evaluate whether the reported findings are robust to this analytic choice.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants

issues.description: The design in Experiment 1 is functionally a retro-cue paradigm — a spatial cue is presented after the memory display to direct attention to one item. A large literature on retro-cues shows they can selectively protect items from subsequent interference, alter confidence calibration, and interact with working memory capacity. None of this literature is cited or discussed, yet it is directly relevant to the design logic and to the interpretation of the 'interference' condition.
issues.quote: the memory cue appeared after a blank of 0.75 seconds (Short) or 3 seconds (Long), for 0.5 seconds, on a blank screen. Subsequently, 5 seconds after offset of the memory display, an irrelevant second letter display … appeared for 0.5 seconds

issues.subcategory: inconsistent terminology for cue vs. probe vs. test display
issues.description: The manuscript uses 'memory cue,' 'memory probe,' and 'test display' inconsistently and apparently interchangeably across sections. In the training task a 'cue' indicates a location and a 'test display' is shown for comparison; in the main experiments a 'memory probe' or 'memory cue' both refer to a location indicator, while the actual response occurs from a separate 'response display.' This terminological inconsistency makes the procedure difficult to follow and may obscure procedural differences across experiments.
issues.quote: the memory cue appeared after a blank of 0.75 seconds … The experiment had three memory conditions. In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display … The response display consisted of 6 letters

issues.description: Experiments 1, 2, and 3 each contain an explicitly labelled 'Methods' section. Experiment 4 has no Methods heading; it moves directly from the introduction paragraph to 'Participants.' The Stimuli subsection simply states they were 'the same as in Experiment 3.' The Procedure section mentions online administration but does not report whether the visual-angle specifications were verified given variable screen sizes and viewing distances in online testing.
issues.quote: Experiment 4 … Participants … In this experiment, 95 participants participated … Stimuli … The memory displays and irrelevant intervening screens were the same as in Experiment 3.

issues.subcategory: no sample-size justification for Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: Experiments 1 (N=40 after training exclusion) and 2 (N=290) provide no power analysis or sample-size rationale. The sample size in Experiment 2 is explained as determined by course enrollment rather than by statistical considerations. Large incidental samples can inflate Bayes Factors and produce high sensitivity to small effects. Without a prospective justification, it is unclear whether the sample sizes were appropriate or inflated.
issues.quote: The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course, which explains the large increase in participants compared to Experiment 1.

issues.description: The word 'participants' is misspelled as 'particpants' in the Introduction. While minor in isolation, such errors in a manuscript submitted for peer review suggest the manuscript may not have been thoroughly proofread.
issues.quote: One way to resolve this ambiguity is to test particpants at (at least) two different moments after stimulus offset.
